evidence.title: Implementation of a clinical decision support tool for hypertension in a rural health system
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.effect: High-intensity implementation with monthly check-ins was more effective than low-intensity for repeat BP measurement (aOR 3.45) and recognition (aOR 2.31).
evidence.quote: High-intensity implementation was more effective than low-intensity implementation for repeat BP measurement (aOR 3.45; 1.88-6.33) and hypertension recognition (aOR 2.31; 1.08-4.98).

evidence.title: Academic Detailing to Enhance Adoption of Clinical Decision Support for Patients at Risk of Opioid Overdose
evidence.effect: A general educational email to all providers increased the prescription-to-alert ratio from 32.6% to 51.7%.
evidence.quote: The first academic detailing intervention resulted in a prescription-to-alert ratio increase from 32.6 to 51.7%, a 19.1% absolute increase when comparing the approximately 8 months before and after the email was sent (95% confidence interval [CI]: 16.3-21.9%, p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Barriers and Enablers for Sustaining Nurse-Led Use of Clinical Decision Support Tools for Antibiotic Stewardship: Qualitative Study
evidence.outcome: Nurse-perceived barriers and enablers to sustaining CDS tool use, including training needs
evidence.effect: Ongoing need for training and support emerged as one of five themes among 22 nurses and nurse leaders interviewed about sustaining the CDS tool.
evidence.quote: Five themes emerged: (1) importance of staffing stability and capacity, (2) impact of dedicated clinic resource availability, (3) variable nurse readiness with CDS-guided clinical care, (4) influence of openness to change and a nurse-supportive clinic culture, and (5) ongoing need for training and support.

commentary.bottom_line: Two studies suggest that continued contact with clinicians after go-live may improve use of decision support, but neither isolates recurring AI refresher training, and both measure clinician process outcomes rather than patient harm. Six sources endorse the practice, mostly frameworks and commentaries.

perspectives.view: A cluster RCT with 9155 patients found higher odds of repeat BP measurement (aOR 3.45) and hypertension recognition (aOR 2.31) with monthly check-ins. That arm was a bundled high-intensity implementation, not refresher training alone, so directness is limited. A pre-post study without a comparator adds very low certainty support. Certainty is rated low.

Both studies measured whether clinicians acted on alerts or findings. Neither measured misuse, overreliance, or patient harm over time. The rise in prescription-to-alert ratio from 32.6% to 51.7% suggests clinicians responded more to alerts after education, but the data do not show whether the added prescriptions were appropriate.

Nurses interviewed about sustaining a decision support tool named ongoing training and support as one of five themes, which shows the need persists after launch. The single educational email tested was a one-time contact, and the study did not report whether its effect lasted, so decay after reinforcement remains untested.

The cluster RCT enrolled rural patients, which offers some information on settings with fewer resources. No study reported results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and no study examined whether reinforcement changed performance gaps across patient groups.

The two tested formats differ in staffing demand. A single email reached 2161 providers, while the trial used monthly check-ins that require recurring staff time. Neither study reported cost, staff hours, or the time clinicians spent in training, so the resource trade-off between light and intensive reinforcement is unknown.

No study asked patients about their experience or trust, and none reported whether reinforcement affected patients' access to a clinician's own judgment. The trial's gains in BP remeasurement and recognition may benefit patients with undetected hypertension, but this link rests on process measures.

commentary.research_gap: No study has randomized clinicians to recurring AI-specific refreshers, briefings, or multidisciplinary rounds versus go-live training alone and followed knowledge retention, appropriate versus inappropriate reliance, and patient outcomes over months to years, with costs and training frequency reported.
commentary.underserved_note: The cluster RCT included rural patients. No test of the practice reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, so the effect of post-go-live reinforcement in those settings is unknown and may differ where staffing and training time are constrained.
